title: Writing for Scott, manager Harvey Bacall and the ten-dollar bonus
summary: On tour Handy wrote charts for Dorothy Collins and others, was paid ten dollars extra by manager Harvey Bacall, and left over it.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yeah, those are his. I joined his quintet and then it became a big band and we went on tour. He had a manager named Harvey Bacall who really took advantage of me. One night he found out that I could write--they were having me write for them-- as we toured around, we'd get into town and Raymond would say to me I need a chart on "My Mama Done Told Me" for Dorothy and I want to do it in the show this afternoon. He'd tell me that in the morning. So I'd get in my hotel room and write the chart for him and Dorothy would sing it.
Which Dorothy?
Dorothy Collins. She was fifteen years old at the time, travelling with her mother and singing with the band.
He married her later on.
She later on was on the Hit Parade. As a matter of fact, his brother was the Hit Parade band Mark Warnow.
He took it over when Mark died.
Did he?
Right.
But then at the end of the week at salary time, I would find ten dollars added to my salary for the charts. That was really offensive to me.
Were you copying it too?
Yes. I really was deeply hurt by that. Then I went to Ray and I said Raymond this is not nice of you people to do this

to me, how can you actually think that you can pay a man ten dollars for all this work. He didn't want to know about it. Harvey handles that, and talk to Harvey. I couldn't handle these fast talking people; I have trouble enough today handling a fast talker, except that I have no problem recognizing them anymore.
That's half the battle.

Yeah. Those people have dug holes in my life with their fast talking. However, that's what finally caused the separation between Raymond and myself. Harvey Bacall, his manager, decided that he could write music too so he started to write little charts, and my God, they were terrible.
Were any of your things recorded?
By Raymond?
Yes.
I don't know. No, not actually on record, but I've had some--I don't
have them anymore; I may have them but I don't know where they are. I used to keep air checks of the stuff I wrote for him, I'd take it off the air, hold onto them.
He used to do my stuff in theaters, after I left him I'd go watch the band in a show, in a theater and he was using my stuff.
At this point, if you ever find them, it would be worthwhile to have them to add to this document we're creating here.
How could they be useful? You mean the stuff that I wrote for Raymond?
Yes, sure; it's part of you in any case.
The only value it would have is historical.
That's what I'm talking about.
Anything about me is valuable historically.
That's why we're here.
Oh, I keep forgetting.
You have now become famous, if not rich.
This is our secret though.
